If you're a single mother with small children with a long commute and you're working a couple of jobs and you don't have a babysitter, you're not coming to the town hall meeting. Policy that works for the urban residents may not work for the rural residents. Policies that work for one type won't work for another. Things that work for a 40-year-old man with a college degree don't work for an 80-year-old. They don't work for an eight-year-old. They don't work for people who've only been here a year. We have new cars in our underground in the metro. It's absolutely hysterical. They didn't want to have a lot of congestion near the doors. So they've got a lot of that overhead pipe you can hold on to. If I reach like this, I can touch the pipe. I can't reach it. If we actually took the route of understanding the lived experience of other people, taking those as challenges and building the solutions, whether they're technical or not, The technologists have to be at the table. You have to start working with people. And that's it. Thank you, Susan, for the great talk. So now we have time for some discussion. Any questions, comments? I'm from the Vienna City Library, and I was wondering if you took a look at the smart city strategy of the city of Vienna. If you look at what's written about smart cities and you look at the rhetoric, it's all about the technologies. It's, even with Wi-Fi access, it's a much deeper problem. The only way we got people to talk to us is on the research team, we included Sherry Parks, who has been deeply engaged in the West Baltimore community her entire life. Yeah, it takes deep and prolonged engagement. Yeah, hi. I'm actually working for Siemens, so thank you for mentioning Siemens. And I was just passing by. The governments very often don't. So there is an imbalance. And what are your ideas of changing that? Excellent question. And I do have some ideas. As I said, businesses are doing exactly what we've told them to do. But in this situation, what we need to do is figure out how do we align the interests of business? with the interests of people. And it's going to mean that there are going to be some hard changes. But it comes down to the question of whether society is here to serve business or business is here to serve society. That's why they actually want a strong legal system. They want a strong banking system. That's why they don't go put their facilities in Mogadishu. Failed states are not good for businesses. We could do something like the legal system does in the U.S., where you have a right to... Big companies, big legal firms do what's called pro bono, and there's a lot of social pressure. I think one of the important points you made was reminding us engineers that people tend to use technology in a different way than we would use it. Or couldn't we have the imagination of an airplane crashing into a skyscraper in New York or into illegal persons using Bitcoin if that's an anonymous way of doing transfers? So I, there's a group in my faculty that works on socio-technical cyber security and they actually, the stuff that's unclassified that they can talk about is terrifying and I choose not to work in that field because of it. But yeah, part of it is a lack of imagination. I really do think so. And part of it is they can imagine it, but they think it's too unlikely. And, yeah, people have a failure of imagination, and they don't pay attention because they think it's improbable. Just some examples, please. Cities that are doing it well. It's interesting. As I say, I think about smart cities projects more so than cities as a whole. One thing is to get out of your local community. Get out of just talking to the people who are on the same hallway as you. And theories about, why it's starting earlier every year and lasting longer. Be more of an omnivore. Go read other stuff. Go talk to other people. What we find, people always think about doing interdisciplinary collaborations, that what you need is kind of a Facebook or a Tinder where I know... how to do ethnography, and you know how to make sensors, so I'll find you in a database, and we'll decide that we want to do something together. That's not how scientists do collaborations. They meet each other, they decide whether they like each other, and if they like each other, they find something, they find a project they can work on together. How do you create situations where scientists run into each other, faculty run into each other? It's becoming more and more of a problem, certainly in the U.S., because we've lost a lot of social organizations. segments.text: So welcome to the lecture series on digital humanism. In April this year, we from the Faculty of Informatics here at TU Wien organized together with the Vienna Science and Technology Fund and with the city of Vienna a workshop with more than 100 participants from different countries and different disciplines.

And so the goal of this workshop was to reflect the complex interplay of technology and humans, and more importantly, to think of ways how we could influence this interplay in a positive way for a better society. The Vienna Manifesto on Digital Humanism as a call for action and reflection in this regard is one outcome of this workshop.

And so you see it everywhere here, so you can take one, you can read it, and you can support it by going on the website and sign it. And yeah, so the link to the website you find on the printout. And another outcome of the workshop is a lecture on digital humanism for master students that is taking place now here at TU Wien, but we organize it together with the University of Vienna.

And the public part of this course is now this public lecture series, which is also supported by the Vienna Science and Technology Fund. Yes, and today this lecture series starts, and I'm very honored to welcome Susan J. Winter as the first speaker of this lecture series.

And Susan is Associate Dean for Research and Co-Director of the Center for Advanced Study of Communities and Information at the University of Maryland College of Information Studies. So she has a background in business administration and information systems, so she has a PhD in that area from the University of Arizona.

But she also has a background in organizational psychology, where she has a master's degree from the Claremont Graduate University and also a bachelor's degree from University of California at Berkeley in industrial and organizational psychology. Her research focuses on scientific data work and new forms of cooperative production, living in smart and connected communities.

information and communication technologies and new forms of work, and ethics and emerging technologies. So her work has been supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation and by the Institute of Museums and Library Services, and she has received a high number of competitive grants, a lot of awards, and many recognitions. She's in the editorial board of different renowned journals.

And she's the editor of the computing ethics column of the communications of the ACM. And now we will hear her talk with the title, Kuibono, a sociotechnical view of smart cities. Thank you for that lovely introduction. Can you all hear me in the back? We were fooling around with microphones earlier.

So if it ever doesn't work, start making hand gestures in the back there. Yeah, so I'm Susan Winter, and I actually have been looking at smart cities for a little while and looking at who benefits. My background is interdisciplinary, and so looking at this from a computer science perspective, from an organizational psychology perspective,

I bring a different sort of lens to this. I guess the first question as we think about who benefits is to ask, why do we care who benefits? Basically, the question of who benefits is one of the oldest questions in ethics. And as such, we look at values.

Ethics, what society says is acceptable. Society says some things are just absolutely not acceptable. No fraud, no theft, no murder. But then there are lots of different ethical frameworks. So you may recognize David Hume from the Scottish Enlightenment, and he said benevolence and social virtue are important. That we should be concerned about others and our interrelations with each other, not just because it's good for them.

but because it's terribly important for us. And so we should practice compassion, generosity, and service because we're all part of the same society. You may also ask, why do I care who benefits? My goal has always been to look at quality of life. And within that, I focused on quality of work life. And within that, looking at...

technology and work practices. Why? Because I did my undergraduate degree at UC Berkeley and was doing my master's in organizational psychology at Claremont, and it seemed like there were these things showing up that could really affect quality of work life. These computer things, these personal computers were coming into workplaces.

Robots were coming into manufacturing facilities. Seemed to me like this could have a real impact on quality of work life. Turns out they have a real impact on quality of life as well. Not just because work affects, technology affects your work life and your work life affects your life satisfaction, but also because these things have actually infiltrated into our lives. So I did...

How did I come by this interest in quality of life and quality of work life? It's really, I think, stems from my parents and my grandparents. My mother's people lived in West Virginia in coal country. They weren't miners, but their classmates were. That was terrible work. There's an 11-year-old miner in 1908. My father's father...

was in the garment industry in New York City. He did furs, pelts. That was terrible work. Not because the work itself, but the way we organized it and the way we managed it and the way we controlled it. I spent 20 years as a faculty member in colleges of business and doing things, working in industry, working for Duke Energy, being a program manager, a project manager.

And what I discovered, it took me a long time to learn it, I'm not very smart, I actually don't care about corporate profits. I actually don't care about shareholder value. That made me a very bad fit for business schools. I would have been okay as a fit for business schools in the 1950s, but in the 1970s, Milton Friedman and the Chicago School of Economics was very influential in arguing

that the only goal of business is to make profit and provide shareholder value. That's what drove Reagan. That's what drove Thatcher, drove a revolution in business. I actually really don't care about that. I do care about quality of life, and I love teaching because I love watching the light bulb go off over people's heads, which means I should not be in industry. I should not be in business. I spent four years at the National Science Foundation.

The agency in the U.S. that funds 80% of basic computer science research. They also fund research in other sciences as well. I was in the Office of Cyber Infrastructure, where they funded the big supercomputers. And then I actually cared about people. They found that rather surprising. And then for three years, and then one year in Social Behavior and Economics Directorate, where I actually cared about technology, which...

they found kind of confusing. I found that the interesting stuff I was funding, most interesting stuff was coming out of things called Colleges of Information Studies. Not out of business schools, not out of computer science. So when I left NSF and National Science Foundation, you can come for four years and then you time out. You go back into academia.

I took a job at the University of Maryland's College of Information Studies. Colleges of Information Studies are a little bit weird. We actually care a lot about quality of life. At the University of Maryland, our goal is to harness the power of information so that everyone can improve their world. Sometimes that means you have to change the information.

Sometimes it means you have to change the technology. Sometimes it means you have to change the people. But it's about getting people information to empower them. And we focus on information, how it can be used by people, by teams, by organizations. What do I mean by changing the information? Originally, we were a library school. The information was in books.

and the touchscreen doesn't register your fingers anymore. How do we change the technology so that people can use it? Sometimes you have to change the people. And we provided information as libraries from the beginning, not just...

in libraries, but we had bookmobiles for places where there were roads. And we delivered books on horseback where there weren't roads. We still have the bookmobiles. We work to increase the positive impacts and decrease the negative impacts. But we are always sensitive to questions of equity. We all remember a time a librarian helped us. Why did that librarian help you? Because you needed help. That's what we do. We focus on groups that need help. I went to an iSchool about the time that the Smart Cities movement got started. So I thought, okay, I know about information. Smart Cities are about information. Let's figure out what this is.

I searched smart city definition on Google a couple days ago. 219 million results. Okay, nobody really has a definition of smart cities, but I've picked a couple of good ones here. Wikipedia is generally, the Wikipedians are pretty diligent in making sure that they collect the information that's needed and present it.

And they're saying an urban area that uses different types of electronic Internet of Things sensors to collect data, get insights from that data, manage the assets, resources, and services efficiently. You guys all know what the Internet of Things is, right? Small, lightweight sensors, long battery life, networks for moving to 5G with low latency, allowing real-time control.

You've got data, metadata, analytics, reports, notifications, visualizations. Stop me if any of this seems surprising. Who's doing this? Engineers, computer scientists, material scientists. They're working on the cutting edge in universities like this, in companies like Siemens. They're creating new technologies to improve efficiency. Well, maybe Wikipedia is just one example.

How about Technopedia? The first thing that comes up actually on Google if you search for smart cities definitions. It's basically the same thing. They're all saying new technologies for efficiency. That that's what smart cities are all about. And yeah, it should enhance quality of living for citizens, but through smart technology. So the technology is the one that's driving it.

It's going to be more efficient and it's going to make everybody so happy. There are a couple of different ways of approaching this in terms of smart cities technologies. I always look at them and think about whether the goal that's being pursued, what's the role of the people? Are the people being engineered out of the system or are they central to the system?

And we see as you look at the various users of these smart cities technologies, for some of them, we have engineered people or trying to engineer people entirely out of this system. So the sensor senses the amount of traffic and it automatically tells the traffic signals to change. Smart buildings, they sense whether there's somebody in them. And if there isn't, then...

They reduce the amount of heating, ventilation, air conditioning, and they turn off the lights to save energy. No people involved. By the way, we have that in our building. More trouble. You guys have that? You're sitting there working at your desk and the lights go off. I'm still here. We've had people who've taped it over because the sensor is actually, they're not line of sight of the sensor. It's hitting the back of the screen of their computer.

So yeah, those things are awesome for people, not so much. Self-driving cars. We've engineered the people out of the system. Sometimes the users are city planners. So they're using the information to figure out where road construction should happen, where parking spaces should be, what the tolls ought to be based on usage. So if it's very busy, they did this recently on one of the main freeways coming into Washington, D.C. If you're trying to come in,

during rush hour in the morning, and you're a single person in the car. Highest it got up to was $48 to get into the city. It's hit that more than once. Yeah, people were really shocked. Sometimes the users are government workers, where they'll get a text or an alert saying, we need you to go empty this trash bin. It's full now. Sometimes the users are residents. They're putting up kiosks with Wi-Fi.

local maps, internet access, the ability to charge your device. So there's some variance in terms of the technologies that we have. And what are they promising us? Technical innovations are supposed to lead to these desired solutions. So if we have self-driving cars, then we're going to reduce congestion, parking spaces, fuel use.

Traffic cameras and sensors adjust automatically. We're reducing congestion, pollution, fuel use, increasing toll revenue. Buildings with the cameras and sensors conserve energy, reduce costs for government buildings, compacting solar-powered trash cans that signal when full, reduce the collection frequency, odors, rats, government costs. These are all good things. So who's creating these smart cities?

Because whoever's creating them affects who's going to benefit. If you're creating it, you have some power over who's going to benefit. So who's creating the new Internet of Things sensors, information communications technology, data insights algorithms, engineers, computer scientists? Who's disseminating the technology? These are companies seeking profits as vendors. They're going to sell it to the city.

We're not seeing a lot of companies that are just going to give this away. Remember Milton Freeman saying, nope, short-term profits and shareholder value is what drives this.
